title: The defense attorney
hookLine: Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev was well-known for pleading his people's case before God
last: KNOW WHICH POCKET TO REACH INTO.

lines: THE FRIEND WHO TAKES YOUR SIDE.
cards: Some friends always take your side. Call them furious about someone, and they're furious with you. Call them ashamed of yourself, and they say: come on, you were exhausted, anyone would have done that.
Sometimes they're too generous. But you always hang up feeling like someone is on your team.
Long ago, in the town of Berditchev, in what is now Ukraine, a rebbe played that role for his whole people, in the one courtroom that mattered most to him: before God.

teach.b: His name was Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev, a student of the Maggid of Mezritch. People called him the defense attorney of Israel. The Hebrew word is sanegor, an old word borrowed from Greek, meaning an advocate.

teach.h: ONE ADVOCATE FOR EVERY GOOD DEED.
teach.b: Pirkei Avot already uses the courtroom picture: every good deed you do gains you an advocate, every wrong gains you an accuser. Levi Yitzchak decided his job was always to be the advocate. There are many stories.

One morning he saw a wagon driver wrapped in his prayer shawl and tefillin, praying, and at the same time greasing the wheels of his wagon. Anyone else might have scolded him: praying and greasing wheels at once?
Levi Yitzchak looked up and said, in effect: Master of the world, look at your people. Even while they grease their wagon wheels, they're praying to you. Same scene, two ways to see it.
He's remembered for arguing with God, too, out loud, on behalf of suffering people, in the line of Moses, who pleaded for Israel after the golden calf.
In this tradition, that's read not as disrespect but as a kind of love: taking both God and people seriously enough to argue. The stories come from Hasidic tradition and the details vary.
But his reputation is solid: wherever others saw fault, he looked for the defense.

how: Stories of Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev are told especially around Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, the days of judgment, and Jewish teaching encourages judging others favorably, l'khaf zekhut.

o: a judge who weighs good deeds against bad
an advocate who speaks up for the defense
a prosecutor who lists a person's wrongs

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.

s: Levi Yitzchak scolded the wagon driver
he told God: look, even greasing wheels, they pray to you.
arguing with God on behalf of people has deep Jewish roots
Moses pleaded for Israel after the golden calf.
sanegor is a Hebrew word borrowed from Greek
it means an advocate, a defender.

games.q: you see a man praying in his tallit and tefillin while greasing his wagon wheels. what do you say?
o: tell God: look, even greasing wheels, they pray.
games.why: Levi Yitzchak turned the scene into a defense: even at work, his people pray. he always looked for the defense.

practice: Think of someone you've been judging lately, a coworker, a relative, someone in the news, maybe yourself, and picture them doing the thing that bothers you.

Like Levi Yitzchak, look for the defense, the most generous true reading: tired, scared, trying in their clumsy way? If you pray, you can speak up for them in your own words; if not, make their case silently, as well as you can.

wordCard.voice: Sanegor, the Hebrew word for an advocate. Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev always pleaded his people's case before God, and found the good in what others scolded.

orig.note: Hebrew, from Greek: an advocate, the one who speaks for the defense.

carryVoice: Your line: always the defense. Tomorrow, a tailor who argues even harder. Three hundred days, and still walking.

sources.ref: Hasidic tales of Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev
